content: 1. Diagnostic tests must be evaluated for operational aspects, including the expertise required of users, the infrastructure and testing conditions, and the specific characteristics of the assay. 2. The founding members of the Global Harmonization Task Force (GHTF) include Australia, Canada, the European Union, Japan, and the United States. 3. Examples of stringent regulatory assessments include: WHO prequalification for all classes, with a public report. European Union certifications such as EC Full Quality Assurance Certificate, EC Production Quality Assurance Certificate, and EC Type-Examination Certificate. U.S. FDA Class III approvals, including PMA letters or Biologics License Applications (BLA). Health Canada Class IV Medical Device Licenses and CMDCAS-issued ISO 13485 Certificates. Australian TGA Class 4 Licenses, ISO 13485 Certificates, and other quality assurance certifications. Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour, and Welfare (JMHLW) Class III approvals, manufacturer licenses, and recognized foreign manufacturer certifications. 4. If no products meet WHO prequalification or stringent GHTF member reviews, efforts should be made to assess other quality certifications held by the manufacturer. This may involve requesting: A list of all quality reviews conducted on the product. Evidence of compliance with internationally recognized standards, such as ISO 13485. 5. Independent performance evaluations of candidate assays may be published in peer-reviewed literature. The Standards for Reporting Diagnostic Accuracy (STARD) criteria should be used to exclude low-quality studies. 6. Periodic assessments of diagnostic testing algorithms are essential. For example, in HCV testing: Low rates of HCV viraemia in HCV-antibody seropositive individuals may indicate high false-positive rates (poor specificity). Conversely, low seroprevalence rates with a higher proportion of detectable HCV RNA may suggest false-negative results. Such findings should prompt revalidation of the testing algorithm to select assays with improved sensitivity and specificity. 7. Post-market surveillance of diagnostics is critical to ensure ongoing quality, safety, and performance. WHO has established systems for proactive and reactive post-market surveillance, including: In-country lot verification testing before and after distribution. Reporting and evaluation of complaints, adverse events, and corrective actions. 8. Effective quality management systems are essential for hepatitis testing programs. These systems should encompass all testing activities, including those in health and community-based facilities, and incorporate 12 interconnected components such as personnel, equipment, process control, and safety. 9. Quality assurance (QA) frameworks should be integral to all staff roles, ensuring the accuracy of testing, pre-test information, and post-test counseling. QA activities should be planned, implemented, evaluated, and sustained. 10. Quality control (QC) processes ensure that testing procedures are performed correctly, environmental conditions are suitable, and assays function as expected. QC involves pre-analytical, analytical, and post-analytical checkpoints to detect and correct errors before reporting results. 11. All testing personnel must be adequately trained, certified, and supported. Training should include pre-service and in-service education, periodic refresher courses, and ongoing supervision and mentoring. 12. Testing facilities must be well-designed, clean, and safe, with adequate lighting and measures to prevent harm to clients and staff. Universal precautions, waste disposal, and adherence to assay manufacturer recommendations for temperature control are essential. 13. Testing for HBV and HCV markers can occur at various levels of the healthcare system. The complexity of assays depends on infrastructure, staff skills, and operational requirements. Expanded use of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) can improve access at the primary care level. 14. Specimen integrity is critical for accurate testing. Manufacturers’ instructions for specimen collection, storage, and stability must be followed. Serum/plasma specimens are commonly used, but less invasive methods like oral fluid or capillary blood collection may be appropriate in certain contexts. 15. Pre-test and post-test counseling are essential components of hepatitis testing services. Counseling should address the 5 “Cs”: consent, confidentiality, counseling, correct results, and connection to care.
